titulo.texto: Mural “La Sierra Tarahumara,” by Pablo O’Higgins

frase_gancho.texto: The painter of the Purépecha wedding also painted the sierra where the Rarámuri (Tarahumara) live.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the landscape of the sierra, we move on to a festival of the desert. Look for a deer head adorned with colorful ribbons, next to rattles made from gourds and strings of cocoons.

guion_corto.texto: This mural is titled “La Sierra Tarahumara,” also known as “Paisaje tarahumara.” It was painted by Pablo O’Higgins, an artist born in the United States in 1904 who came to Mexico in 1924 at the invitation of Diego Rivera. The museum opened in 1964 and commissioned murals from several artists to help visitors understand each culture. O’Higgins received three commissions, including this one. The Sierra Tarahumara is the part of the Sierra Madre Occidental, in Chihuahua, where the Rarámuri (Tarahumara) live. They are the people of the violin, of the yúmari, and of the great races you learned about in this hall. O’Higgins painted workers, peasants, and Indigenous peoples throughout his life. Here he devoted a wall to the landscape of the sierra.

guion_largo.texto:
The museum opened on the seventeenth of September, 1964, and murals were commissioned from several artists for its halls. This is recorded in the catalog of the artworks of that year, prepared by the historian Justino Fernández. In this hall, the wall went to Pablo O’Higgins, and its subject is the sierra of the Rarámuri.

The title is “La Sierra Tarahumara,” or “Paisaje tarahumara.” Both names speak of a place. It is the Sierra Madre Occidental, in the state of Chihuahua, a region of canyons and pine forests. The Rarámuri live there, the people of the violin and of the yúmari.

O’Higgins was born in Salt Lake City, in the United States, on the first of March, 1904. In 1924 he came to Mexico City at the invitation of Diego Rivera. He worked as his assistant on the murals of the Secretaría de Educación Pública and of the Escuela de Agricultura de Chapingo. In 1961 the Mexican government granted him Mexican nationality as an honor. He died in 1983.

His life resembles his painting: he was always close to the countryside and to ordinary people. In the late 1920s he took part in the Misiones Culturales, which brought teachers and art to rural towns. In La Parrilla, Durango, he decorated an open-air theater. In 1937 he was one of the founders of the Taller de Gráfica Popular, together with Leopoldo Méndez and Luis Arenal. It was a group of printmakers that used art to speak about workers, peasants, and Indigenous peoples. He also taught at La Esmeralda. The Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes notes that his painting grew freer over the years. He moved closer to abstraction without losing his social commitment.

There are more of his works in this same museum. You have already seen the Purépecha wedding in the hall of the Purépecha. There is also another mural about the Purépecha people, titled “Luchas del pueblo tarasco.” With the sierra of the Rarámuri, that makes three, and all three deal with Indigenous peoples of today and of the past.

The title does not detail which scene he painted, so look at it yourself. Start with the horizon: do you see mountains, canyons, trees? Then look for whether there are people and what they are doing. Think about what you already know about the sierra. There, people run for hours, play the violin, and dance the yúmari to ask for rain. A wall can sum up all of that at once.

There is a contrast worth noting. A painter born far away, in Utah, portrayed peoples of Michoacán and Chihuahua for this museum. Something similar was done by [Leonora Carrington](mna_s19_mural_carrington), born in England, with the Maya of Chiapas. It is a view from outside. That does not take away from the mural’s value, but it reminds us that the display cases let the objects made by the peoples themselves speak.

Before moving on, give this wall a minute. After the violin, the woven plate, and the wood, it is a chance to see the landscape of one of these peoples.

texto: Look for the horizon: what shape do the mountains or the canyons have?
See whether there are people in the scene and notice what they are doing or what they are wearing
Compare the colors of this mural with those of the Purépecha wedding in the hall of the Purépecha

texto.pregunta: Myth: The museum’s murals are ancient paintings made by the peoples they depict.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are works by twentieth-century artists, such as Pablo O’Higgins, commissioned in 1964 to help visitors understand each hall.
